# A1 · Walking Skeleton {.unnumbered}

The core now runs on the computer. This chapter runs the same state machine on the board, with *skeleton adapters* that stand in for the modules. This is called a **walking skeleton**: a version that does almost nothing, but goes through every layer, from `main.cpp` to deep sleep.

## Skeleton adapters

On the board, each interface needs an implementation. In this step, they are deliberately minimal:

| Interface | Skeleton adapter | Behavior | Replaced in |
|-----------|------------------|----------|-------------|
| `IClock` | `SystemClock` | ESP32 system clock, invalid after a power-on, no alarm | A2 |
| `ISensor` | `NullSensor` | All values missing | A3 |
| `IStorage` | `SerialStorage` | Prints the row on the serial port | A3 |
| `INetwork` | `NoNetwork` | The connection always fails | A4 |
| `IMaintenance` | `NoMaintenance` | Returns at once | A5 |
| `IPower` | `Esp32Power` | Real deep sleep, safety timer only | A2 (alarm), A5 (button) |
| `ILog` | `SerialLog` | Prints each state entered on the serial port | Kept |

The clock is the most interesting one. The ESP32 system clock keeps counting during deep sleep, but restarts at `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` after a power-on. Any time before 2026 therefore means that the clock was never set, which gives a simple `isValid()`. The time of the last `setTime()` is kept in RTC memory (`RTC_DATA_ATTR`, see [Deep Sleep](../../PoC/Phase-02/01-deep-sleep.qmd)), the only memory that survives deep sleep:

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/src/adapters/SystemClock.h"}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## C++: `static_cast` and `static`

- **`static_cast<uint32_t>(...)`** converts a value to another type, here the `time_t` of the system clock into our `uint32_t`. It does the same as the C cast `(uint32_t)`, but it is visible when reading, and the compiler refuses the dangerous conversions that a C cast would accept.
- **`static`** before a variable outside any function limits it to the current file, so that the name cannot clash with another file.
:::

The power adapter is the only one that really drives the hardware in this step. It prints the sleep plan and the awake time, then enters deep sleep with the safety timer (see [Deep Sleep](../../PoC/Phase-02/01-deep-sleep.qmd)):

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/src/adapters/Esp32Power.h"}
```

`Serial.flush()` waits until every character has left the serial port: without it, the end of the message could be lost when the chip goes to sleep.

## main.cpp

`main.cpp` only creates the adapters, gives them to the state machine, and runs it. For the demo on the bench, the interval is shortened to 20 seconds.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/src/main.cpp"}
```

The clock object is named `rtcClock`, not `clock`: `clock()` is already a function of the C standard library.

## Expected output

Build and flash the firmware, then open the serial monitor. The repository has moved on since this step: to flash exactly the version of this chapter, first run `git checkout v0.2.0`, and `git checkout main` to come back afterwards.

```bash
pixi run pio run -d firmware/paws -t upload
pixi run pio device monitor -d firmware/paws
```

Here is the output of the first two wake-ups after a power-on, as printed on the board (the awake time may differ slightly on yours):

```text
-> BOOT
-> MEASURE
-> STORE
   row: 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z time_valid=0 T=nan H=nan P=nan
-> UPLOAD
   no network before step A4: connection failed
-> SCHEDULE
-> SLEEP
   RTC alarm: no, button: not wired before A5, timer: 20 s
   awake for 495 ms
ets Jun  8 2016 00:22:57

rst:0x5 (DEEPSLEEP_RESET),boot:0x13 (SPI_FAST_FLASH_BOOT)
configsip: 0, SPIWP:0xee
clk_drv:0x00,q_drv:0x00,d_drv:0x00,cs0_drv:0x00,hd_drv:0x00,wp_drv:0x00
mode:DIO, clock div:1
load:0x3fff0030,len:1344
load:0x40078000,len:13964
load:0x40080400,len:3600
entry 0x400805f0

-> BOOT
-> MEASURE
-> STORE
   row: 1970-01-01T00:00:21Z time_valid=0 T=nan H=nan P=nan
-> UPLOAD
   no network before step A4: connection failed
-> SCHEDULE
-> SLEEP
   RTC alarm: no, button: not wired before A5, timer: 20 s
   awake for 495 ms
```

The path is the one of an invalid clock: the upload is attempted at every wake-up to reach NTP (F6 · Flag unreliable time), and fails without blocking the schedule (N1 · No data loss). With no RTC alarm, the safety timer is the only wake-up source (N2 · Always wake up again).

Between the two wake-ups, the lines from `ets Jun  8 2016` to `entry` are printed by the boot code of the ESP32 itself, before our firmware starts. `rst:0x5 (DEEPSLEEP_RESET)` confirms that the chip woke up from deep sleep, and not from a reset.

The second row is timestamped `00:00:21`: the 20 seconds of the timer, plus the time to wake up and boot. The system clock kept counting during deep sleep.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---------|---------------|
| `pixi run test` fails because `g++` is not found | The compiler comes from the pixi environment (`cxx-compiler`). Run the command through `pixi run`, not with a `pio` installed elsewhere. |
| The first lines of each wake-up are missing in the monitor | The monitor reconnects after each reset. Press the board's `EN` button to restart from a power-on and watch the first cycle. |
| The time restarts from `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` at every wake-up | The chip was reset instead of waking up from deep sleep (for example by the monitor, or by a power interruption). Only a power-on or reset restarts the system clock. |
| No output after flashing | Check that the monitor speed is 115200 (set by `monitor_speed` in `platformio.ini`). |

## Next Steps

The skeleton runs, but still measures nothing and has no real clock. In step A2, [DS3231 Clock](02-1-ds3231-clock.qmd), we write the DS3231 clock adapter: real timestamps, alarms on the 15-minute grid, and the wake-up by the `EXT0` pin.
